## 📌 Outlining Your Process

[video](https://www.loom.com/share/55fe516a9ad74cbd812599d75ca9cc03)

# **Coaching Offer Process Builder**

### **1. The Big Picture**

- What is the main *transformation or result* your coaching program helps clients achieve?
  *(Example: Go from inconsistent content to generating leads daily through authority-driven videos)*

- From start to finish, how many *main phases* does it take for a client to reach that transformation?
  *(Example: 5  Phases → Foundation, Content Strategy, Creation, Conversion, Optimization)*

---

### **2. Step Breakdown**

For each step, explain briefly:

- **Step Name:**

- **What happens here?**

- **Why is it important?**

- **What outcome should be achieved by the end of this step?**

*(Repeat for each step until the entire transformation is covered.)*

---

### **3. Phase Grouping**

Now group your steps into bigger *phases* of your program (typically 3–5).

For each phase, fill out:

- **Phase Name:**

- **Which steps are included?**

- **Goal of this phase:**
  *(What do clients walk away with or accomplish at the end?)*

- **Key Materials/Resources Needed:** 
  *(Modules, templates, call replays, worksheets, etc.)*

- **Actions the Client Must Take:** 
  *(What must they complete to move forward?)*

- **What You (the Coach) Do in This Phase:**
  *(What’s expected from you—calls, feedback, reviews, accountability?)*

---

### **4. Phase Progression**

- What needs to happen before a client can move from one phase to the next?
  *(Example: Submit onboarding deliverables, complete worksheet, implement system, etc.)*

- How do you track that progress or verify completion?
  *(Example: Review form, tracker, or feedback check-in)*

---

### **5. Final Outcome**

- Once all phases are complete, what *final transformation* should your client confidently have achieved?

- What proof or deliverables show that they’ve succeeded?
  *(Example: A working content system, a launched offer, 5 booked calls/week, etc.)*

## 📌 Ideating The Fulfillment

[video](https://www.loom.com/share/c1ba483908e64dad9e0ff5e1d8eaf480)

# **Coaching Offer Blueprint (SOP)**

## **1. Program Overview**

- **Program Length:** [e.g., 12 weeks coaching + lifetime course access]

- **Offer Structure:**
  - Done-With-You (Coaching) 
  - Do-It-Yourself (Course + Resources)
  - Done-For-You (Templates/Assets, optional)

**Purpose:** Provide clarity on what students receive, how they’re supported, and the transformation they’ll achieve.

---

## **2. Done-With-You: Coaching Structure**

### **A. Coaching Schedule**

- **Coaching Days:** [Choose 3 days per week – e.g., Mon/Wed/Fri]

- **Availability Window:** [e.g., 5–6 hours per day available for sessions]

### **B. Group Coaching**

- **Format:** [Live group calls, Q&A style, peer learning]

- **Frequency:** [e.g., 2 group calls per week]

- **Purpose:** Address common questions, share solutions, create community accountability.

### **C. 1:1 Coaching**

- **Frequency:** [Weekly 1:1 call per student]

- **Condition:** Students unlock each call only after completing deliverables from the prior week.

- **Purpose:** Tailored guidance for their specific situation, tied directly to their progress on the roadmap.

### **D. Ongoing Support**

- **Platform:** [Discord/Slack/FB group]

- **Support Method:** Daily Q&A, feedback threads, and direct answers from coach.

- **Objective:** Ensure students can get help between calls, keep momentum, and feel supported.

---

## **3. Do-It-Yourself: Course Material**

### **A. Content Library**

- **Modules:** Step-by-step trainings aligned with the 12-week roadmap.

- **Format:** [Videos, worksheets, checklists]

- **Focus:** Take students from setup → implementation → scaling.

### **B. Roadmap Integration**

- Every DIY module matches the week-by-week coaching process.

- Students can always revisit training to reinforce learning.

### **C. Self-Paced Access**

- **Access Level:** Lifetime access after the 12-week live coaching ends.

- **Updates:** [Specify if ongoing updates are included].

---

## **4. Done-For-You: Resources & Assets**

### **A. Pre-Built Resources**

- **Guides/Workbooks:** [Templates, SOPs, worksheets]

- **Tools:** [Swipe files, scripts, plug-and-play frameworks]

### **B. Application**

- Designed to save students time (no starting from scratch).

- Aligned directly with course modules and coaching calls.

---

## **5. Accountability System**

- **Progression Rule:** Students cannot book the next 1:1 call until they complete deliverables from the prior call.

- **Tracking:** [Notion board, Google Sheet, or internal tracker to log deliverables].

- **Coach Responsibility:** Enforce progression to keep students accountable and ensure results.

---

## **6. Deliverables Summary (Fill-in)**

- **Coaching Calls:** [X group calls per week, 1x weekly 1:1 calls]

- **Support Channel:** [Discord Q&A + daily support]

- **Course Material:** [Lifetime access, structured by roadmap]

- **Resources:** [Templates, SOPs, guides, swipe files]

- **Transformation Promise:** [State the end goal clearly – e.g., “Go from ____ → ____ in 12 weeks, with tools for lifetime growth”]

---

## **7. Pricing & Offer Terms (Fill-in)**

- **Pricing Options:** [One-time, payment plans, tiers]

- **Guarantee (if any):** [Money-back, results-based, etc.]

- **Enrollment Process:** [Call → Payment → Onboarding → Access granted]

---

## **8. SOP Checklist (For Any Coach)**

1. Define coaching days & availability.

1. Set group call cadence.

1. Lock in 1:1 call progression rules.

1. Build course roadmap modules.

1. Create DFY resources to cut setup time.

1. Launch support community.

1. Clarify deliverables & end transformation.

1. Finalize pricing & enrollment steps.

title: Dream Follower/ICP Sheet
markdown:
> **Important: Go into detail**

These are your fans, which is what your brand is going to attract - they have the same characteristics, goals, values and resonate with you

---

> **Dream Follower:**

- **Who are they, what’s their story, what do they look like?** - a dream follower for me would consist of someone that picked up a camera at a young age preferebly doing sports and saw being a cameraman as a side hustle and they started up doing maybe high school football around 14, 15 years old and is trying to take it to the next level. Mainly based in places where the entertainment/sports/music industry is at examples : miami, LA, NYC, houston, orlando, etc or planning to move there some day.

- **What are they passionate about?** - theyre passionate about photography and videography. Creating valuable content for clients to post on social media. They like to network with people and always finding ways to learn more about the creative space. Preferably, to have a personal brand and dont care to post their face on insta.

- **What are their goals, dreams, and desires?** - they want to learn how to shoot and work with high respected people in the industry. whether thats pro athletes, celebrities, rappers, influencers, etc. they would like to be making a solid income while proving to their parents that this can actually work for a future career, not needing school. they would want to be connected to the entire creative space, work with the biggest guys in the industry and grow their personal brand. to be “known” as well, kind of to be known as that guy who shoots for so and so.

- **What are their deepest fears?** - deepest fears i would say that would be not knowing how to operate a camera when first starting, not knowing how to color grade. they can be overwhelmed with doing free content, and dont know how to make money/what to charge. they might think that they need expensive gear to start off. making and building a personal brand can be one to, people scared of showing their faces for their brand because they think the content wont blow up and they might get made fun of.

- **What are their struggles?** - the struggles i would say would be they dont know how to have retainer clients, or keep clients from coming back not just a one and done process. they might not know how to network properly, or they dont talk to anybody when they at the gigs. maybe when theyre in rooms, they get shy start acting weird and nervous around professionals etc. sometimes theyre unprofessional without realizing it like they will promise work by such and such date and they dont get it done so it looks bad on them. somestimes they don't communicate with clients fast , no contracts, no invoices, no llc. sometimes they overwork themseleves becausse they dont know what to charge or how to value their work. some are also just stuck ina. horrible city for this whole creative industry. they might think its geographically impossible.

> **Within your fanbase these are the people that you are selling to and that you want to buy**

> **ICP (Ideal Customer Profile):**

- **How much are they making** - an ideal customer would be making around $300-5k a month.

- **What business/service are they providing** - they provide videography, photography, and social media services. they shoot for brands, athletes, sports, real estate, lifestyle shoots.

- **Current situation** - Their current situation could be that they're kind of just stuck in that high school football or high school sports in general, photography and videography. They don't know how to escape it and get to the level that I'm operating at with celebrities and artists and stuff like that that they want to be at. Maybe they're making not that much money and they would like to increase that.

- **Desired outcome** - So the desired outcome with that would be to start operating and dealing with higher-level clients like NBA players, maybe college athletes, celebrities in their city, and just making some more income, maybe getting some retainer clients as well. 

- **Perceived problems** - 

So some perceived problems could be maybe that they think they need better gear. Maybe their city is too small and there are no celebrities in their city or NBA athletes and stuff like that. They don't have any connections where you need to know somebody in order to grow in the creative space. I feel like they're kind of just invisible. They don't have a personal brand or any content up on their page showing their face to actually get to that level that they want to get to. I think they don't do any outreach or networking consistently. Talking to everyone is literally the whole cheat code that they're not doing.

- **What makes a customer a bad fit?** - A bad customer would really just takes this as a side hustle or a hobby. Kinda doesn't wanna go too crazy with it and doesn't mind staying in the high school football, high school sports photography and videography. They're kind of capped at a certain level of money and they don't plan on growing that anytime soon. They're kind of good with what they're making right now and they're doing it as a side gig. They're not posting on social media. That's the biggest part. Posting your work and portfolio, I think, is very important and if my clients or my customers aren't doing that then they're a pretty bad fit. If they're not willing to learn or go the extra step with just knowledge in general with this, I don't think they're a good fit. I would just need people that actually want to learn and want to go all out on this and really want to further their career or whatever they want to do with this.

- **What limiting beliefs does your ICP have?** - Some limiting beliefs, I would say, would be that some people think they need better gear before they could start networking and just putting themselves out there. They think that they're too late because everyone's a videographer nowadays and stuff like that and they didn't hop on the wave early enough. Or they think they need to know somebody to get into the industry. Maybe for personal branding if they pose their face and everyone sees it, they'll get laughed at and stuff like that. Maybe they don't know what to quote customers and clients.

title: Brand Identity Sheet
markdown:
> **Why will people love you for you**

- **What is your story?** → I was born in Miami. I played soccer for around 10 years, and then I played football for two years. I have Cuban roots, and I have Cuban parents. I started filming when I was around 15 with a Canon R7 that my brother's fiancée lent to me. The way I got into it was that I was playing football, and one of my friends would buy pictures from me. I thought it was pretty cool that he was doing that, and he was making a little bit of money. I picked up my brother's fiancée's camera. She lent it to me for around a month, and then from there, I just started doing high school football games, or middle school football games. I was doing sports in high school, and I was making a little bit of money, but I knew I could take it to the next level. I didn't have any connections, and nobody in my family was in the industry, so nobody really handed me anything. At first, my first-ever actual shoot was my old soccer team. I had gone there, and I was doing free work a lot of the time. I was doing free work at high school football games as well, just because I kind of liked it and it was something different that I had never done. There is a point where people kind of just saw me as this new photographer guy, and people didn't like me sometimes as well. To be honest, a lot of the guys that were in the game for a few months, or a few years, kind of just looked at me like I'm this trash kid. I did think about stopping at one point, but I kept picking up the camera, and I met the right person to get me into an FIU game. I met the athletic director for FIU, and he kind of was the first person to believe in me with this. I shot FIU football games, and I connected with a lot of the videographers on campus, along with a lot of other creatives that are on Instagram and stuff like that. From there, I started building a portfolio outside of high school football. That was the first, I would say, decently bigger client that I had, even though I wasn't getting paid for it. From there, I just kind of talked to everyone in every room that I got in. I talked to everybody. From there, I met one of the athletic directors for the University of Miami. He helped me get into University of Miami basketball. I shot a few games for University of Miami basketball, and then I would post that for my portfolio and stuff like that. I would do a lot of outreach as well. I reached out to Davion Mitchell's manager, and he got back to me. They were doing some workouts at the University of Miami, so I would go out there and work for free a lot of the time. I would kind of just show up every day until the season. During the season, his manager actually gave me some tickets to cover the NBA for De'Veon. That's how I got into the NBA and the Heat. Additionally, I saw my boy Lucas doing social media, and his content was doing very well. I kind of hopped on the content thing and the personal branding content, and it really did blow up my page. I'm at around 65,000 followers now. A little bit before this, while this was all happening, Baller League reached out to me before their launch of the first season. They wanted me as a photographer for Baller League. That's where I met Speed, Marlon, Drewski, J Balvin, Kit Super, Ronaldinho, and a lot of other guys. They opened up doors for me, connecting with each and every single one of them, and that opened up doors for me to work with Arcángel in front of literally a stadium of 50,000 people at 16 years old. They also opened up doors for me to work with Speed Slips. They actually reached out to me, saying that they need somebody to help them out for a few streams. I came out there and helped out, and hopefully we're building something long term as well. My content has been doing very well. Now I've done like 20 million views, and each and every day I'm just trying to push for harder and bigger. That's basically my story.

*{Insert Loom of your  Story For Team Members To Watch & Get Ramped On}*

- **What are your values?** - My values, I would say, are hard work kind of beats talent. Talking to everyone is definitely my biggest value. Never gatekeep information. I think that people that help people will always get opportunities back to them. For example, if I give my friend a gig, he always repays me with a gig that he can't make it to, stuff like that. That's why I'm kind of making this course. It's really just to show people how to get it done. I think families come first, but definitely putting people on when you're already doing well and staying humble no matter what is very important to me. Delivering everything that I promise regarding work every time, I think, is very important.

- **What are your beliefs?** - I would say my beliefs are that if you put your mind to it and you work hard at it, then you get anything achieved. You just need to not quit. You need to make your connections along the way in order to get access to the right rooms. You don't really need the best gear. You need to start with what you've got and your budget. I think that conversations and just networking bring a lot of opportunities, but definitely the biggest one is that consistency beats talent every single time. Consistency and networking, knowing the right people, beats talent. 

- **Your personality?** - I feel like my personality would be. High energy, Funny, Easy to talk to, Outgoing, Communicative, Very direct. I kind of like to have fun with my job. I'm kind of a guy that talks to everybody in the room. A bit motivational, but I like to keep it real about the grind and just keep going hard at it. I think I would say I'm very humble.

> **Your visual design**
> - **Describe your style** - I would say my style is just kind of cinematic and clean. I like a lot of the BTS content, so the behind-the-scenes energy when I'm doing videos.
> - **Favourite colors** - I like the Miami Vice colors, like the teal and the pink, but also I like a little bit of red. It would signify working with the Miami Heat. Kind of whatever you think is best for the funnel, but that's kinda my idea of it. Something that would just match the logo too.
> - **Editing** - Regarding the editing, I like more of the cinematography, kind of just cinematic edits, some quick cuts, hooks in the first couple of seconds. I like to do some cinematic captions on the screen, along with the cinematic colors. The sound design as well, I think, is big.

> **Brand Outliers**
> - **What makes you different? i.e special talents, play sports, where you live, can you speak multiple languages?** - Well, what makes me different? I'm based in Miami, which is one of the biggest entertainment and sports cities in the world, I would say. For artists, too. I speak English and Spanish, so I kind of work double the rooms, and I can reach double the audience. I have access to a lot that a lot of creators never touch in their lifetime. At 16 years old, whether it's NBA, Miami Heat, Speed, working alongside Marlon, Drewski, and a lot of people, my audience kind of already knows me for that: pick up the camera, talk to everyone, because that's kind of been my message from the start. I also played soccer for 10 years Im athletic.

> **Vehicle**

- **Explain your business** - 

My business operates like this: I freelance, so I shoot anything that comes my way. I travel for gigs as well. People would just hit me up for gigs that they have here in Miami or in LA and stuff like that. I'll fly out or I'll go to the gigs, and I'll shoot whether they need photography, videography, or event recaps, kind of all of the above. I do social media management as well for brands, and I do content creation in general for these brands, athletes, and teams. When I'm done with the shoots, I go back home. I usually deliver everything within 48 hours. I would edit the photos, edit a recap, or edit the videos, and I'll deliver that to them. Those will be the deliverables, depending on what they need. That's how budget comes into play and pricing for people.

- **What is your goal with that business?** - 

My goal with this business: right now, I'm 17 years old, and I've been able to very much breach into the entertainment industry with this. I've been able to talk to a lot of people in the industry and get a lot of knowledge from people that are older than me, which I think is very, very important and advantageous. My goal with this business, really, is to build it to a different level and a different scale. I want to get to the point where the whole city of Miami, especially, knows me and what I do. I can make an agency where I send out other videographers and other photographers to gigs that I don't want to go to anymore, and I'm still making a cut out of it.For example, if they tell me, "Oh, shoot a high school game," kids DM me for high school games. I'm like, "Okay, yeah, you could all point a photographer that can go for me through my agency," and then I'll take a cut for that. Obviously, for the bigger-level clients, my NBA clients, my celebrity clients, I'll take care of them and stuff like that. I just keep stacking, keep going at it, keep building, definitely. I want to get my Instagram to another level. I'm at 65,000 followers. I want to get it to at least 200,000 and just keep building the personal brand as well.

- **Why are you running that business?** - 

Well, right now I'm running this business for a few different reasons. I'm doing it to really break into an industry that I want to work in in the future, 100%. I'm doing it for the connections, the people that I meet every day. You never know that they could open doors for any other opportunities in anything, for example, whether it's real estate or just other opportunities. I want to get into the real estate industry as well very soon. With that, I could ask a lot of people that are very well connected for real estate and that already own that and already know a thing or two, and kind of pick their brain about it. Also, I'm running the business to make money. I think that's important. I still live with my parents and stuff like that, so I just want to keep stacking money so that I can see what I do in the future.

- **What type of value can you provide around that business?** - 

I think that I can provide value in definitely operating a camera, editing, and color grading. A lot of the business side that nobody really teaches about, like:

- retainer clients

- pricing

- contracts

- invoices

- delivering on time

- networking

- how to talk to everyone and actually follow up

Access to stories and behind-the-scenes from rooms that I've been in and a community that you're not going to be grinding alone in anymore. You're going to have people in your corner, and you could ask questions, definitely

title: New Opportunity Breakdown
markdown:
---

> **Important: Go into detail**

**Describe one shocking or highly emotional moment on your journey (date, place, who was present).** - definitely being on speeds stream during the world cup was a highly shocking one. When I got called up for it, it felt unreal. to then being in the background on the stream with speed and jamal in the car. slipz was pointing the camera at us during the stream, parents watching the stream from home.. it felt pretty cool definitely.
> 

**Paint a picture of your daily life before chasing today’s result (job, income, routine).** - 
my daily life before this to be honest was no job, kind of just depending on my parents for everything financially till about 10th grade when i started. I wasn’t really making any money, I had a reselling business that I started but didnt go that far with it to pay for my own expenses. I would go to school and go back home, sleep, wake up and get on the video games to just repeat that 5 days a week. on weekends id play video games a lot on discord with my boys and hangout on weekends.

**State the external goal you were pursuing and the internal fears you felt then.** -
>
> I wanted to shoot the big athletes and celebs in the world and be known for my work. inside though I was scared that I was wasting my time that I didn't know anybody so I'd never get in, and that everybody watching me try was gonna clown me.

**What specific obstacle—or “wall”—proved your old approach was broken?** -
>
> i think when i first shot some university of miami basketball games i realized that this can be more than just a hobby or a side job.

**How did that failure impact your finances, relationships, or self-worth? (Give concrete examples.)** - 

So to be honest I havent really had any “failures” throughout this journey so far. Theres been low months and high months but something that can stand out was when I was going through a breakup and lowkey it was sad because I broke up with this girl I really liked coming back from a cruise with her and I was shooting at the heat arena that night and we broke up a few hours prior to the game. I thought of myself just like leveling myself up to be honest and how can I make my page go crazy. I had 3-5k followers at the time and I knew at my age and the access that I have, its nearly impossible. I knew i can use that to my advantage to build a social media following. So, that night I cooked up some ideas and I posted the next morning a reel that blew up and got like 2 million views. it was “16 years old and this is my job”, with cinematic audio. from then i think it really triggered me that this was the way to go about it. Posting personal brand content and work and just improving my life in general kind of distracted me from thinking about all the breakup situatuion to. at the time i didnt really have a good relationship with my parents either so I kind of just used content to distract myself a bit and build something.

**Where were you when the breakthrough occurred, and who or what triggered it?** - 
a few days after the breakup i saw my boy lucas posting personal branding content and I kind of liked the idea of it so I started hopping on it as well and started growing my page as is.

**In one sentence, describe the New Opportunity you saw.** - I saw by me posting content, it will open doors because high level clients want high level videographers and social media people in their corner. I noticed that ever since I was doing good on the instagram, celebrities or brands start hitting me up more, Im getting recognized and its eventually making me more money.

**List the first three actions you took immediately after that aha moment** - built a content strategy for reels, I would post at least 2 reels a day. I also tried to network and do outreach as I was growing my brand, Focus on bettering my craft so I can keep up with the clients im dealing with.

**What major conflicts did you face after committing to the new path?** - Laziness is definitely a big one. Definitely when it came to posting content I tried to be as consistent as possible with 2-3 reels a day but at some point i run out of ideas and I would get a bit lazy to then only doing 1 reel a day or 0 at times to. i got drained a bit, but the content side of the brand is the only thing that will make you grow and consistency is key to success for this industry. Something i also struggled with was promising false delivery times to clients. for exmaple i would have a week that id be super busy and promise them deliverables within 48 hours when I couldnt get that done in 48 hours. 

**What measurable result did you finally achieve? (Numbers, time saved, etc.)** - 
well i started seeing drastic growth in my social media numbers, getting millions and millions of views and traction on my page for being a 16 year old with nba access in the whole world. Doign work with celebs to gained me a lot of traction, to the point that ballerleague, the company i worked with for speed, druski and marlon and all these guys, they actually told me to stop posting personal brand content using the talent because i was getting more numbers than the ballerleague insta page lol. they told me that they were gonna fire me if i kept posting . they then wanted to meet with me to become the community manager and director of content.

**What internal transformation did you experience (identity shift, confidence boost, outlook)?** - definitely a identity shift, i felt like i kind of found my passion for this. confidence definitely was boosted as well, people started recognizing me in public, kids at my school would start asking me for photos lol.

---

> **Skills you’ve mastered (rank your top three).** - Personal brand content, networking, photography/color grading

**Do you already use frameworks, checklists?** - Yes

**In one sentence, what future do you want your audience to experience? (The Goal)** - 
I want them to live off a camera and to be in rooms they used to watch through a screen
**Why does that matter to you personally?** - bc i was watching therough the screen at one point and had no one to guide me or show me a path to get to what i wanted to do.

**Five years from now, describe the movement you hope to lead in a tweet-length sentence** - i would want to lead a whole generation of camera people that networked their way up and took over the industry.

**What old way(s) of doing things frustrate you most in your niche?** - people often gatekeeping gigs. for example if i cany make it to a gig ill send my boy to cover for me. some people just say their not available bc their scared they might steal their client.

**What old way(s) of doing things frustrate you most in your niche?** - 

**List 3 common myths holding people back** - people think you need to know somebody when u get to know somebody by talking to them. ppl think u need expensive gear when really you just gotta put urself out there on the map with the gear you have is fine. 

**What tools / programs / gurus are folks currently using that leave them stuck?** - lowkey random youtube tutorials that may just confuse them more. and by far the biggest one that i experience first hand is school. Its so braindead, like you're in a classroom filled with kids with the same knowledge as you and you cant go on ur own pace. definitely film school and regular tv production classes in highschool are bullshit.

**From your perspective, why do those vehicles fail?** - they fail because, yea u learn a bit of editing, how to use a camera, maybe some lighting but thats only like half of the whole operation. the otherhalf is the networking, personal brand, content, putting yourself out there and connecting with other professionals in the industry and haveing a portfolio.

**Single biggest outcome you want your students/clients to achieve (make it concrete: money, time, health, etc.)** - I would want my client to first of all start making some more money, whether thats at least one retainer client or concurring gigs a month. That and a personal brand that they are posting every day face on the camera, name known in their city, to the point clients start coming to them

**Time horizon you believe is realistic for that outcome (days, weeks, months).** - I would say it depends on how hard you go at it. for me it took around 3 months to really settle in and dial on the content side but i also had the access which boosted my stuff a lot. i think regularly it can go from 3 months-12 months to really get the content side going its all about consistency. regarding the retainer clients its just outreach. could take around 2 weeks.

**Key milestones between day 1 and the outcome (bullet them).** - 

-master camera movements, audio, lighting, etc
-editing a color grading locked in
> -personal brand dialed in
>
> -Networking routine running on autopilot outreach, follow up, repeat
>
> -bigger rooms

**Non-negotiables your program would require from clients (daily actions, tools, mindset).** - pick up the camera every day, post every day, outreach every day, show ur face, follow up with everybody u meet, deliver on time every time, and going hard at it all times even when things slow down
